1a.html:
Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a year.

Answer: by total GDP Bangladesh is a fairly big economy, but per person it is not.

Why it counts as big (aggregate size)

  1. Size. Nominal GDP was about USD 446 billion in 2023 (USD 460 billion in 2022), roughly the 35th largest in the world, and higher (about 25th) at purchasing power parity.
  2. Regional weight. It is the second-largest economy in South Asia after India (about USD 3.6 trillion), ahead of Pakistan (USD 341 billion in 2023).
  3. Fast growth. GDP rose about eightfold from USD 54 billion in 2001, with growth of about 6 to 7% a year (5.82% in 2023-24).
  4. Large market. About 172 million people, the 8th largest population, and exports of USD 40.8 billion, mainly ready-made garments.

Why it is not big (per person and in welfare)

  1. Small world share. About 0.4% of world GDP (about USD 105 trillion) against 2.1% of world population; the US economy is about 60 times larger.
  2. Low income per head. GDP per capita is USD 2,675 (GNI per capita USD 2,784, higher mainly because of remittance income from abroad), about one-fifth of the world average: a lower-middle-income country.
  3. Size comes from population. \text{GDP} = \text{GDP per capita} \times \text{population} = 2675 \times 171.6\ \text{million} \approx \text{USD } 459\ \text{billion}: many people with modest output each.
  4. Development lags. HDI 0.670, rank 129 of 193 (medium); poverty 18.7% and extreme poverty 5.6% (2022).

Conclusion: Bangladesh is a big, fast-growing developing economy by total GDP, but not a rich one. GDP measures the size of output, not the welfare of each person.
pts: Defines GDP: market value of final goods and services produced within the country in a year
Gives a clear stance: big in total size but not per person (either stance earns this if justified with data)
Total GDP about USD 446 to 460 billion (2022-23), in roughly the world's top 40 (about 35th; any rank from 30th to 40th, or the higher PPP rank, is accepted)
Regional comparison: second in South Asia after India, ahead of Pakistan
Growth: about eightfold since 2001, about 6 to 7% a year
Large population (about 170 million) and export base as sources of size
Per capita GDP about USD 2,675 (or GNI USD 2,784): lower-middle income, far below the world average
Small world share (about 0.4% of GDP against 2% of population); size comes from population, not productivity
Development indicators: HDI 0.670, rank 129 (medium), or poverty 18.7%
Concludes: big developing economy by total GDP, not rich per head; GDP measures size, not welfare
1a.src: Dimensions of economic development (v3), slides 3-7, 20, 30-35; Ch 2 Comparative development, slides 3-6; Standard textbook treatment
1a.watch:
• Rankings change with the year and the source (IMF, World Bank, worlddata.info) and with the exchange rate; quote a year and say "about". The aggregate values here come from the slides; the world rank, world totals and India's GDP are standard 2023 values.
  • The slides give FY 2023-24 values (fiscal year, July to June) and calendar-year chart values; 446 and 459 billion are both right for their periods.
  • On hum-dim slide 31 the legend reads "Series2" and "Series5": the purple line (446 in 2023) is Bangladesh, the orange line (341) is Pakistan.
  • A one-sided "yes" or "no" loses marks; the question asks for a justification, so show both the aggregate and the per-head view.

1b.html:
The Harrod-Domar model is a functional relationship in which the growth rate of GDP depends directly on the saving rate and inversely on the capital-output ratio. Output is proportional to capital, Y = AK with A = 1/c, so it is also called the AK model; capital is the only constraint (labour is assumed abundant).

Symbols. Y is GDP and K the capital stock. c is the capital-output ratio, the units of capital needed to produce one unit of output a year; its incremental form \Delta K/\Delta Y is the ICOR. S^G and I^G are gross saving and gross investment, and s^G = S^G/Y is the gross saving rate. \delta is the depreciation rate, the fraction of the capital stock that wears out each year.

Assumptions: c and \delta are constant, output is proportional to capital, and saving equals investment (closed economy, no government).

Step 1. Production function. Output is proportional to capital, so the average and incremental ratios are equal:

Y = \frac{1}{c}K \quad\Rightarrow\quad \Delta Y = \frac{1}{c}\,\Delta K, \qquad c \equiv \mathrm{ICOR} = \frac{\Delta K}{\Delta Y}

Step 2. Capital accumulation with depreciation. Capital grows by gross investment less the capital that wears out:

\Delta K = I^G - \delta K

Step 3. Substitute Step 2 into Step 1:

\Delta Y = \frac{1}{c}\left[I^G - \delta K\right] = \frac{1}{c}I^G - \frac{1}{c}\,\delta K

Step 4. Saving finances investment. I^G \equiv S^G = s^G Y, and from Step 1 K = cY, so \frac{1}{c}\delta K = \delta Y:

\Delta Y = \frac{s^G Y}{c} - \delta Y

Step 5. Divide by Y:

\boxed{g = \frac{\Delta Y}{Y} = \frac{s^G}{c} - \delta}

With the net saving rate s = s^G - c\delta this is the simple form g = s/c (slide equation 3.7).

Interpretation of the variables

  • g: the growth rate of total GDP, the outcome the model explains.
  • s^G: the gross saving rate. Growth rises with it; each extra point of saving adds 1/c points of growth. This is why the stages approach saw raising saving (15 to 20% of GDP) as the key to take-off.
  • c: the inverse of the productivity of capital (1/c is extra output per unit of investment). A higher c means less efficient capital and slower growth, so growth depends as much on how well capital is used as on how much is invested; technical progress lowers c.
  • \delta: part of gross saving only replaces worn-out capital, so each point of depreciation lowers growth by one point; with s^G \le c\delta there is no growth.

Example (slide 18): with s^G = 20\%, \delta = 3\% and c = 2.5, g = 0.20/2.5 - 0.03 = 5\%; a 9% target needs s^G = (0.09 + 0.03) \times 2.5 = 30\%.
pts: Defines the model and the symbols (Y, K, c as capital-output ratio or ICOR, s^G, \delta) and states the assumptions (constant c, saving equals investment)
Step 1: Y = K/c, so \Delta Y = \Delta K / c with c = \Delta K/\Delta Y
Step 2: capital accumulation net of depreciation, \Delta K = I^G - \delta K
Step 3: substitutes to get \Delta Y = (1/c)(I^G - \delta K)
Step 4: uses I^G = S^G = s^G Y and K = cY, so (1/c)\delta K = \delta Y
Step 5: divides by Y to reach g = s^G/c - \delta, and notes the net form g = s/c
Interprets g as the growth rate of GDP
Interprets s^G: growth rises with saving (each point adds 1/c), the basis of the saving-led take-off
Interprets c: inverse of capital productivity; higher c means less efficient capital and slower growth
Interprets \delta: depreciation absorbs part of saving and lowers growth one for one
1b.src: Ch 3 Classic theories, slides 3, 8-18; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 160-162, 185
1b.watch:
• Step 4 needs K = cY: the average capital-output ratio equals the incremental one only because output is proportional to capital. Say so; it is the step students skip.
  • The depreciation term is \delta, not \delta/c: (1/c)\,\delta K = \delta Y, and dividing by Y leaves \delta.
  • Older texts write the capital-output ratio as k (g = s/k). The slides use c to avoid confusion with k, capital per worker, in the Solow model. Either symbol is fine if defined.
  • The model ignores labour and technology explicitly and treats c as fixed; these are its main criticisms (saving is necessary but not sufficient).

2a.html:
The progress. Poverty (national upper line) fell from roughly 70 to 80% in the early 1970s (an approximate estimate) to 48.9% in 2000 and 18.7% in 2022 (extreme poverty 34.3% to 5.6%). Since 2000 infant mortality fell from about 64 to about 21 per 1,000 live births, maternal mortality from about 440 to about 155 per 100,000, and life expectancy rose from 65.1 to 73.6 years (below 50 around independence).

Main drivers

  1. Steady growth and structural change. GDP grew about 5 to 7% a year for three decades. Ready-made garments created about 4 million jobs, mostly for women, raising family incomes and women's status.
  2. Remittances from millions of migrants raised rural consumption, schooling and housing.
  3. Agriculture. High-yielding rice with irrigation and fertiliser made the country nearly self-sufficient in rice and kept food cheap.
  4. Family planning. Contraceptive use rose from 8% to about 62% and fertility fell from about 6.3 to about 2 births per woman, so families had fewer dependants and more to spend per child.
  5. Low-cost health programmes. Immunisation (EPI), oral saline for diarrhoea, community clinics, skilled birth attendants and health visitors cut child and maternal deaths; improved sanitation now reaches about 94% of people.
  6. Education, especially of girls. Free primary schooling and the female secondary stipend raised literacy to 77.9% and delayed marriage and childbearing.
  7. NGOs and microfinance. BRAC, Grameen Bank and others delivered credit, health and schooling to the rural poor and empowered women.
  8. Infrastructure and protection. Rural roads, electricity (access 47% in 2009 to 94% in 2019), mobile phones and mobile money, social safety nets and cyclone shelters reduced vulnerability.

Conclusion: growth raised incomes, but the social gains came mainly from cheap, wide-reaching public and NGO programmes and from women's empowerment, which worked together.
pts: Describes the progress with figures (poverty, infant or maternal mortality, life expectancy)
Driver: sustained growth and RMG jobs, especially for women
Driver: remittances
Driver: agricultural growth and food security (rice Green Revolution)
Driver: family planning and the fertility decline (contraceptive use, TFR about 6.3 to about 2)
Driver: low-cost health programmes (immunisation, oral saline, community clinics, skilled birth attendants)
Driver: education, especially girls' stipends and literacy
Driver: NGOs and microfinance, women's empowerment
Driver: infrastructure (roads, electricity, mobile), safety nets or disaster preparedness
2a.src: Dimensions of economic development (v3), slides 4, 7, 65, 70, 74, 77, 79, 86; Ch 6 Population, slides 40, 46, 51; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 599, 802
2a.watch:
• The 1971 baselines (poverty roughly 70 to 80%, life expectancy below 50 years) are not on the slides and estimates differ; any reasonable value stated as approximate is fine. The slide series start in 2000.
  • Infant and maternal mortality values are read off the course charts (slides 77 and 74, from UN and macrotrends data); other sources differ by a few points (BBS gives an IMR of 27 and a life expectancy of 72.3 years for 2023, slide 4).
  • "Drivers" asks for causes: list each driver with how it worked, not only the outcomes.

2b.fix: • Slide 25 of the Dimensions deck says 10.4% of Bangladesh's population is multidimensionally poor, with intensity 42.2%. Since \mathrm{MPI} = H \times A, 10.4% is the MPI value (0.104), not the headcount: H = 0.104/0.422 \approx 24.6\%, about a quarter of the population (the Global MPI tables give H = 24.6%).
2b.html:
Poverty here is the share of people below the national upper poverty line (the cost of a basic food and non-food basket); extreme poverty uses the lower line. SDG 1 aims to "end poverty in all its forms everywhere" by 2030; the national 2030 targets are poverty below 12% and extreme poverty below 3%.

Are current measures sufficient? Only partly. They have worked: poverty fell from 48.9% (2000) to 18.7% (2022) and extreme poverty from 34.3% to 5.6%, through growth, RMG jobs, remittances, microfinance, rural roads and electricity, and over a hundred safety-net programmes. But they are unlikely to end poverty:

  1. Slowing pace. Poverty fell 1.2 points a year in 2010-16 but 0.93 in 2016-22. If it keeps falling by the 2016-22 proportion (about 4% a year), it is about 13% in 2030, just above the target. GDP growth fell to 3.49% in FY25 and private investment is stuck near 23% of GDP.
  2. Hard-core and vulnerable poor. The remaining poor live in char, haor, coastal and hill areas and urban slums; many near-poor fall back after floods, illness or inflation.
  3. Poverty in all its forms. About a quarter of people are multidimensionally poor (MPI 0.104), 24% of children are stunted, and households pay 73% of health costs out of pocket.
  4. Weak delivery and finance. Safety nets are fragmented, small and poorly targeted; tax revenue is below 8% of GDP; inequality is widening.

Additional strategies for SDG 1

  • Inclusive, job-rich growth: diversify beyond RMG (agro-processing, light engineering, ICT) and support SMEs and rural non-farm work.
  • Reformed social protection: one digital registry, life-cycle allowances, cash through mobile banking, cover for the urban poor, and self-targeting workfare (food for work, EGPP).
  • Graduation programmes for the ultra-poor: an asset transfer plus training and coaching (BRAC model), then microcredit.
  • Human capital: quality education and TVET, nutrition and conditional cash transfers, health insurance to cut out-of-pocket costs.
  • Climate resilience: climate-smart farming, embankments and shock-responsive transfers in coastal and char areas.
  • Redistribution: progressive taxation (tax-to-GDP above 12%), land and credit access for women and the landless.

Conclusion: current measures will keep poverty falling, but ending it in all its forms by 2030 needs these extra strategies.
pts: Defines poverty and extreme poverty (upper and lower national lines) and SDG 1 as ending poverty in all its forms by 2030
Credits the progress (48.9% to 18.7%, 34.3% to 5.6%) and the drivers behind it: growth, RMG, remittances, microfinance, safety nets

Takes a reasoned position on sufficiency with evidence, for example the slowing pace (about 13% by 2030 on trend against below 12%) and slower GDP growth; a reasoned "yes, if growth recovers" also earns this
Names the hard-core and vulnerable poor: lagging regions (char, haor, coastal, hill, slums) and near-poor hit by shocks
Notes poverty in all its forms: multidimensional poverty (MPI 0.104, about a quarter poor), stunting 24% or out-of-pocket health spending 73%
Notes weak delivery: fragmented, poorly targeted safety nets, low tax-to-GDP or widening inequality
Strategy: inclusive, job-rich growth and diversification beyond RMG
Strategy: reformed social protection (registry, life-cycle, digital cash, urban cover, workfare)
Strategy: graduation programmes or microfinance for the ultra-poor
Strategy: human capital (education, TVET, nutrition, health financing)
Strategy: climate resilience for vulnerable areas, or another sound strategy such as land and credit access or progressive taxation
Concludes that the measures help but must be extended to reach SDG 1
2b.src: Dimensions of economic development (v3), slides 7, 25, 65; Bangladesh and the SDGs (2026), slides 5-7, 9-14; Ch 5 Poverty and inequality, slides 55-56, 66-73
2b.watch:
• "Do you believe" asks for your view: give a clear yes, no or partly, then the evidence. A one-sided "yes" with no reasons earns little.
  • 18.7% and 5.6% are HIES 2022 headcounts by national lines, not the World Bank's international line (USD 2.15 a day).
  • The 2030 projection is an illustration, not an official forecast: the 2016-22 proportional decline gives about 13%, a straight-line decline about 11%. Either way the margin is thin, and post-2022 inflation and slower growth make it thinner. A reasoned "yes" is also creditable.
  • Todaro's package (slide 73): correct factor-price distortions, redistribute assets, progressive taxes and transfers, build the capabilities of the poor, and ease the "cognitive tax" of poverty; any of these is a valid extra strategy.

3a.html:
The Lewis two-sector model (W. Arthur Lewis, 1954; formalised by Fei and Ranis) is a theory of development in which surplus labour from the traditional agricultural sector moves to the modern industrial sector, whose growth absorbs it, industrialises the economy and makes growth self-sustaining.

The two sectors

  • Traditional sector: overpopulated rural subsistence farming with fixed land and traditional technology. Lewis assumes surplus labour: the marginal product of labour, MP_{LA}, is zero, so workers can leave without any loss of output. Workers share output equally, so the rural wage W_A equals the average product, TP_A/L_A.
  • Modern sector: urban, high-productivity industry. Employers hire until the marginal product of labour equals the wage, so the MP_{LM} curve is the labour demand curve.

How modern-sector growth works

  1. The urban wage W_M is fixed at a premium over W_A, enough to draw workers to town. At W_M the supply of rural labour is unlimited, so the supply curve W_M S_L is horizontal.
  2. With capital K_{M1}, demand D_1 meets supply at F: employment is L_1, output is the area 0D_1FL_1, wages are 0W_MFL_1 and profits are W_MD_1F.
  3. Capitalists reinvest all profits. Capital rises to K_{M2}, demand shifts out to D_2 and employment rises to L_2 at the same wage; the larger profits are reinvested again (D_3, L_3).
  4. This continues until the rural surplus is absorbed. Beyond this Lewis turning point the rural marginal product is positive, the labour supply curve slopes upward and wages rise.

Result: structural transformation from rural agriculture to urban industry, at a pace set by modern-sector capital accumulation. It fits Western history and China's recent growth.
pts: Defines the model: surplus labour moves from traditional agriculture to the modern industrial sector, which absorbs it and industrialises the economy
Traditional sector has surplus labour with MP_{LA} = 0, so labour can be withdrawn without loss of output
Rural wage W_A is set by the average product (equal sharing), not the marginal product
Urban wage W_M fixed at a premium above W_A, with an unlimited (perfectly elastic, horizontal) labour supply
Modern-sector employment where MP_{LM} = W_M (in words or on a diagram), output split into wages and profits
All profits reinvested, capital rises, labour demand shifts out and employment grows (L_1 to L_2 to L_3) at a constant wage
Continues until the surplus is absorbed: the Lewis turning point, after which the supply curve rises and wages increase
Outcome: structural transformation from agriculture to industry, with an example (the West or China)
3a.src: Ch 3 Classic theories, slides 22-26; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 163-166
3a.watch:
• W_M is not the subsistence wage itself: it is a fixed premium (Lewis suggested about 30%) over the rural average income W_A. Both lines are flat.
  • Rural labour is in millions and urban labour in thousands on the textbook figure: the modern sector starts small.
  • The rural wage equals the average product, not the marginal product (which is zero). Mixing these up loses the surplus-labour argument.

3b.html:
Rostow's stages-of-growth model (1960) holds that every country passes through the same sequence of stages on the way to development:

  1. Traditional society: subsistence farming, barter, limited technology.
  2. Preconditions for take-off: farm surpluses, infrastructure, education, banking, an entrepreneurial class.
  3. Take-off: a sharp rise in saving and investment, leading manufacturing industries, political change.
  4. Drive to maturity: diversification, innovation, less reliance on imports.
  5. High mass consumption: durable consumer goods; services dominate. In 1971 he added a sixth stage, the search for quality.

My view: relevant as a description, not as a blueprint.

Why it is still relevant

  • Investment matters. Its core message, formalised by Harrod-Domar (g = s/c), still holds: South Korea's investment rose from 15% of GNI (1965) to 37% (1990) as it passed through take-off and the drive to maturity. Bangladesh's investment of about 30% of GDP supported 6 to 8% growth in the 2010s.
  • Structural change and leading sectors are real: labour and output still shift from agriculture to industry and services, often led by one industry (garments in Bangladesh, electronics in East Asia).
  • A simple framework to locate a country and set saving and investment targets.

Why it is limited

  • Necessary, not sufficient: capital did not produce take-off in many aid-receiving countries. The Marshall Plan worked in Europe because markets, transport, skills and efficient government already existed; Rostow assumes these.
  • One linear path: countries skip or merge stages (India's services-led growth, mobile phones without landlines), and the boundaries are vague and hard to test.
  • Ignores the international setting: late developers face established competitors, unequal trade and finance, and capital flight (the dependence critique).
  • Narrow goal: mass consumption as the end point ignores poverty, inequality and the environment, now central to the SDGs.
  • Weak prediction: Rostow picked India, not South Korea, for take-off.

Conclusion: the model is partly relevant. It rightly stresses investment and structural change, but development today also needs institutions, human capital and sustainability, which it neglects.
pts: Defines the model: all countries pass through the same sequence of stages to development (Rostow, 1960)
Names the five stages in order with a feature of each (the sixth stage is a bonus, not required)
States a clear position with reasons; "relevant", "not relevant" or "partly relevant" all earn this if argued
Relevance: saving and investment drive growth (Harrod-Domar), with an example such as South Korea or Bangladesh
Relevance: structural change and leading sectors are still observed, or the model is a useful simple framework
Limitation: investment is necessary but not sufficient; the Marshall Plan worked because institutions, skills and markets already existed
Limitation: a single linear path; stages are skipped or merged, and boundaries are vague
Limitation: ignores the international setting (dependence, competition, unequal trade or capital flight)
Limitation: narrow goal of mass consumption, ignoring poverty, inequality or the environment
Limitation: weak predictive power (India rather than South Korea) or another sound criticism
Conclusion consistent with the position taken
3b.src: Ch 3 Classic theories, slides 3-7, 19-21, 34-35; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 159, 162-163, 174, 181
3b.watch:
• "Do you think" asks for a view. Describe the stages briefly; most marks are for the reasons.
  • Rostow's own take-off test was net investment rising from about 5% to over 10% of national income; Todaro describes take-off as saving 15 to 20% of GDP. Quote either with its source.
  • The Bangladesh figures (investment about 30% of GDP, 6 to 8% growth before 2020) are approximate, from official national accounts; growth has slowed since.

4a.fix: • Slide 25 of the Dimensions deck says 10.4% of the population is multidimensionally poor. With intensity A = 42.2\% and \mathrm{MPI} = H \times A, 0.104 is the MPI value; the headcount is about 24.6%.
4a.html:
Development is the process by which a society moves from a condition of life widely seen as unsatisfactory to one that is materially and spiritually better. It is a multidimensional process: it involves major changes in social structures, popular attitudes and national institutions, as well as faster growth, less inequality and the eradication of poverty.

Dimensions

  1. Economic growth: rising national output, productivity and income per capita (GDP or GNI growth), with structural change from agriculture to industry and services.
  2. Social progress: better health, education and nutrition, less poverty and inequality, social inclusion and gender equality.
  3. Environmental sustainability: growth that does not cost future generations; control of pollution, deforestation and resource depletion.
  4. Institutions and freedom: governance, attitudes, self-esteem and freedom of choice. Sen sees development as expanding capabilities, the "beings and doings" people value.

Measurement. Multidimensional indices track these: the HDI (health, education, income), the MPI (Bangladesh 0.104: about a quarter of people multidimensionally poor) and the 17 SDGs. Income alone misleads: Equatorial Guinea has a GNI per capita of about USD 19,500 (PPP) but an HDI of 0.591, below Bangladesh's 0.608 at USD 3,677.

In essence, development is economic progress accompanied by social well-being and environmental protection, giving a better quality of life for all.
pts: Defines development as a multidimensional process: changes in social structures, attitudes and institutions as well as growth, less inequality and poverty eradication
Economic dimension: growth of output, productivity and income per capita, with structural change
Social dimension: health, education, poverty and inequality reduction, inclusion
Environmental dimension: sustainability for future generations (pollution, deforestation, resources)
Institutional and human dimension: governance, self-esteem, freedom; Sen's capabilities
Multidimensional measures: HDI, MPI (with a Bangladesh figure such as MPI 0.104, or the slide's "10.4%") and the SDGs
Shows that income alone misleads with an example (Equatorial Guinea or similar), or concludes with a better quality of life for all
4a.src: Dimensions of economic development (v3), slides 8-14, 24-25; Ch 1 Economic development (Todaro), slides 5, 16-23, 27; Ch 2 Comparative development, slide 22; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 10-13
4a.watch:
• The course deck gives three dimensions (economic growth, social progress, environmental sustainability); Todaro adds institutions, attitudes and freedom. Naming all four is safe.
  • A short note still needs structure: a definition, the dimensions, a measure and an example.
  • The HDI and income figures are from the 2018 Human Development Report table (2011 PPP dollars); quote them as approximate.

4b.html:
All three criteria rest on discounting: a benefit B_t or cost C_t in year t is worth 1/(1+r)^t of its face value today, where r is the discount rate (end-of-year flows, year 0 = now and undiscounted).

Net present value (NPV) is the present value of benefits minus the present value of costs:

\mathrm{NPV} = \sum_{t=0}^{n} \frac{B_t - C_t}{(1+r)^t} = PV(B) - PV(C)

Accept if \mathrm{NPV} > 0: the project earns more than the opportunity cost of the resources. \mathrm{NPV} = 0 means it earns exactly r. NPV is in taka, additive across projects and the primary criterion.

Benefit-cost ratio (BCR) is benefit per taka of cost:

\mathrm{BCR} = \frac{PV(B)}{PV(C)}

Accept if \mathrm{BCR} > 1, which happens exactly when \mathrm{NPV} > 0. Being a ratio, it ranks projects by efficiency when the budget is limited.

Internal rate of return (IRR) is the discount rate at which NPV is zero:

\sum_{t=0}^{n} \frac{B_t - C_t}{(1+\mathrm{IRR})^t} = 0

Accept if IRR exceeds the required rate. It is found by trial at two rates and interpolation. It is easy to communicate, but ignores scale, can have several values when net flows change sign more than once, and assumes reinvestment at the IRR.

Example. Tk 100,000 now and Tk 40,000, 50,000 and 60,000 in years 1 to 3, r = 10\%: PV(B) = 36{,}364 + 41{,}322 + 45{,}079 = Tk 122,765, so NPV = Tk 22,765, BCR = 1.23 and IRR = 21.6%. All three say accept.
pts: Basis: future flows discounted by 1/(1+r)^t because of the time value of money; year 0 not discounted
NPV defined as PV(B) - PV(C) with the summation formula \sum (B_t - C_t)/(1+r)^t
NPV rule: accept if positive (earns more than the opportunity cost); NPV = 0 means it earns exactly r
BCR defined as PV(B)/PV(C), accept if above 1; agrees with NPV on accept or reject
IRR defined as the discount rate giving NPV = 0, accept if above the required rate; found by trial and interpolation
Compares them: NPV is the primary, additive money measure; BCR ranks under a budget limit; IRR ignores scale or may have multiple values
Illustrates with numbers (for example NPV Tk 22,765, BCR 1.23, IRR 21.6%) or the NPV profile
4b.src: CBA exam note, pp 5-9; Solved problems: NPV, IRR, payback, pp 1-2, 4; Cost-benefit analysis handout, handout parts IV, V, VII and VIII
4b.watch:
• Question 4 prints 35 marks for three short notes, so this note is worth about 11.67; budget the time.
  • The exponent is t, the year of each flow, not n for every term; one handout writes (1+r)^n.
  • BCR is not unique: gross PV(G)/[K + PV(O)] and net PV(G - O)/K give different numbers but cross 1 together. State the convention.

4c.html:
The Human Development Index (HDI) is a composite index, published by UNDP (new form since 2010), that measures a country's average achievement in three dimensions of human development: health, education and living standard. It ranks countries into tiers of human development.

Indicators and goalposts: life expectancy at birth (20 to 85 yr); expected years of schooling (0 to 18) and mean years of schooling (0 to 15); GNI per capita at purchasing power parity (USD 100 to 75,000, taken in logs).

Calculation: each indicator becomes a dimension index, (actual - min)/(max - min), and education averages its two sub-indices. Then

\mathrm{HDI} = \left(I_H \times I_E \times I_I\right)^{1/3}

The geometric mean means a weak dimension is not fully offset by a strong one.

Classes: very high 0.800 and above, high 0.700 to 0.799, medium 0.550 to 0.699, low below 0.550.

Bangladesh: HDI 0.670, rank 129 of 193, medium human development, ahead of India (134) and Pakistan (164).

Assessment: the HDI shows that development is more than income, since countries with similar incomes have very different HDIs. But its equal weights are arbitrary, it hides inequality within a country, and it counts years of schooling rather than learning.
pts: Defines the HDI: a UNDP composite 0 to 1 index of average achievement in health, education and living standard, used to rank countries
Three dimensions and four indicators: life expectancy, expected and mean years of schooling, GNI per capita at PPP
Dimension index = (actual - min)/(max - min) with stated goalposts (fixed, or the slides' observed maxima); income in logs
\mathrm{HDI} = (I_H I_E I_I)^{1/3}, the geometric mean, so a weak dimension is not fully offset
Classes with cut-offs 0.800, 0.700 and 0.550
Bangladesh: 0.670, rank 129 of 193, medium (another recent HDR value with its year also earns this)
Assessment: one strength (beyond income) and one limitation (weights, hidden inequality or quantity over quality)
4c.src: Dimensions of economic development (v3), slides 14-20; Ch 2 Comparative development, slides 13-21; HDR 2019 technical notes, pp 2-3
4c.watch:
• A short note is not a full derivation: the formula, goalposts and classes are enough; a worked example is optional.
  • The Bangladesh value depends on the report: 0.614 (2018 data, HDR 2019) and 0.670 (the slides' value, HDR 2023-24); later reports differ slightly. Quote the report year with the number.
  • Only income is logged; life expectancy and schooling are linear.

5a.html:
The hidden momentum of population growth is the tendency of a population to keep growing for decades after birth rates fall, even to replacement level (about 2.1 births per woman), because a large young population expands the base of potential parents. Like a speeding car after the brakes are applied, it stops only gradually.

Why it happens

  1. High birth rates cannot be changed overnight. Fertility rests on social, economic and religious norms; in Europe the fall took decades.
  2. Young age structure. A wide-based population pyramid means each cohort of children is larger than its parents' cohort. When these children reach childbearing age, the number of couples is much larger, so even two children per couple gives many births, while deaths stay low because few people are old.

Illustration. Take generations of 30 years: 10 million elders, 20 million parents and 40 million children (total 70 million). If fertility drops at once to replacement, each generation only replaces itself: after one generation the population is 20 + 40 + 40 = 100 million, after two it is 40 + 40 + 40 = 120 million. It still grows by 71%.

Link to the demographic transition. Death rates fall first (stage II); birth rates fall later (stage III). Momentum is the long tail of stage III, when growth slows but continues.

Bangladesh. Fertility fell from about 6.3 births per woman (1970s) to about 2.0, yet the population still grows about 1.1 to 1.3% a year, adding about 2 million people a year to about 176 million (2025), because the cohorts born when fertility was high are now parents. A rise in fertility to 2.4 (2025) would add to this.

Why it is critical for forecasting

  1. Projections must use age structure. A forecast from fertility alone understates growth; demographers project cohort by cohort.
  2. Long lead times. Fertility falling today stabilises the population only after two or three generations; at 1.3% a year the population doubles in \ln 2 / 0.013 \approx 52 years.
  3. Planning the bulge. The large cohorts need schools now, then jobs and housing, later pensions; the youth dependency ratio and the demographic dividend depend on them.
  4. Large sensitivity. Small changes in assumed fertility act on a large base, so the UN's 2050 world projection (about 9.7 billion) carries a range of several hundred million.

Conclusion: most future growth in developing countries is already "built in", so population policy must start early and forecasts must be made by age group.
pts: Defines hidden momentum: population keeps growing after birth rates fall, even to replacement, because a large youthful population expands the base of potential parents
Reason 1: high birth rates cannot be lowered quickly (social and institutional norms; decades in Europe)
Reason 2: young age structure (wide-based pyramid); larger cohorts of parents give many births even at two children per couple, while deaths stay low
Illustrates the effect, for example a cohort example (70 to 120 million at replacement fertility) or the speeding-car analogy
Links momentum to the demographic transition (death rates fall first, birth rates later; growth continues in stage III)
Bangladesh evidence: fertility near replacement (about 2.0 to 2.2) but growth still about 1.1 to 1.3% a year, or the 2025 rise to 2.4
Forecasting: projections must be by age cohort; fertility alone understates future growth
Forecasting: long lead times before stabilisation, or doubling time \ln 2 / r
Forecasting: planning for schools, jobs, housing and pensions; dependency ratio or demographic dividend
Forecasting: sensitivity to fertility assumptions, or concludes that much future growth is already built in
5a.src: Ch 6 Population, slides 8, 13-17, 40, 46, 48; Dimensions of economic development (v3), slide 4; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 340-345
5a.watch:
• Replacement fertility is about 2.05 to 2.1 only where nearly all girls survive to childbearing age; with high child mortality it can exceed 3.
  • The slides give different Bangladesh growth rates: 1.33% (2023, Dimensions deck slide 4) and about 1.1 to 1.2% (mid-2025, population deck slide 48); both are right for their sources and years. Doubling time is about 52 years at 1.33% and about 60 years at 1.15%.
  • The cohort example is illustrative; any correct example or a clear pyramid argument earns the credit. The question says "explain", so a drawn pyramid helps but carries no separate marks.
  • Population growth rate is births minus deaths (plus net migration) per person; do not confuse it with the total fertility rate.

5b.html:
International trade is the exchange of goods and services across national borders. Countries gain from it in the following ways.

  1. Specialisation by comparative advantage (Ricardo). A country gains by specialising in the good it makes at the lowest relative (opportunity) cost, even if it is less efficient in everything. Example: Bangladesh needs 2 hours for a unit of cloth and 10 hours for a machine; Germany needs 1 and 2 hours. A machine costs 5 cloth in Bangladesh but 2 cloth in Germany. At a trading price of 1 machine for 3 cloth, Bangladesh saves 4 hours per machine and Germany saves 1 hour per 3 cloth: both gain.
  2. Use of abundant factors (Heckscher-Ohlin). A labour-abundant country exports labour-intensive goods, which raises the demand for, and the wages of, its abundant factor.
  3. More output and consumption. World output rises, and each country can consume a bundle outside its own production possibility frontier (PPF).
  4. Access to what cannot be made at home: fuel, raw cotton, capital machinery and technology.
  5. Larger markets and competition: economies of scale, pressure on firms to be efficient, cheaper inputs and more variety for consumers.
  6. Technology and learning: exporters learn from foreign buyers and partners, as early Bangladeshi garment firms did.
  7. Foreign exchange for growth: export earnings (USD 40.8 billion, about 84% from ready-made garments) pay for imported capital goods, easing the foreign-exchange constraint on investment.
  8. Jobs and income: trade puts idle labour to work ("vent for surplus"); the garment industry employs about 4 million people, a large share of them women.

Conclusion: trade raises income and growth for all partners. The gains are not automatic or equally shared: they depend on the terms of trade, diversification and domestic policy.
pts: Defines international trade as exchange of goods and services across borders
Comparative advantage: specialise in the lowest opportunity-cost good; both gain even when one country has an absolute disadvantage in everything (a numerical example is not required)
Factor endowments: labour-abundant countries export labour-intensive goods, raising the return to labour
World output rises and countries consume beyond their own PPF
Access to goods, raw materials, capital goods or technology not available at home
Economies of scale from larger markets, competition, lower prices or more variety
Technology transfer and learning from foreign buyers or partners
Export earnings supply foreign exchange for imported capital goods and growth
Employment and income, for example garment jobs for women in Bangladesh, or vent for surplus
Concludes that the gains depend on terms of trade, diversification and policy
5b.src: Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 669-675, 687; Dimensions of economic development (v3), slide 6; Standard textbook treatment
5b.watch:
• Comparative, not absolute, advantage is the core idea: a student who explains only "a country exports what it makes cheaper" misses the main point.
  • The topic has no course slides; the theory follows Todaro chapter 12 and the trade values come from hum-dim slide 6 (FY2023-24). The 84% garment share and about 4 million garment jobs are commonly cited estimates; quote them with "about". Figures earn no marks of their own: the mechanism does.
  • "Briefly explain" wants benefits, so the critique of free trade (falling terms of trade for primary exports, North-South inequality) earns at most the closing remark.

6a.html:
Human capital is the productive capacity embodied in people (skills, knowledge, health), built by spending on education, training and medical care. Health and education are interconnected because they play a dual role in development: they are ends in themselves (core values, Sen's capabilities) and inputs to the production function. Above all they are investments in the same person, so each raises the return to the other.

How health raises the return to education

  1. Healthy, well-fed children enrol earlier, attend more and learn better.
  2. A longer life lengthens the period over which schooling pays off, raising its rate of return.
  3. Better health lowers the "depreciation" of education capital: a sick worker cannot use his skills; deaths of school-age children waste school spending.
  4. Evidence: cheap deworming in Kenya cut school absence by about a quarter, at about USD 3.50 per extra year of schooling.

How education raises the return to health

  1. Health programmes rely on literacy and numeracy learned in school (reading prescriptions, following treatment).
  2. Schools teach hygiene and sanitation, and train doctors, nurses and health workers.
  3. Educated women marry and bear children later, which improves maternal and child health.
  4. Better-educated mothers have healthier children at any income level, mainly through health knowledge.

Significance

  • Income alone is not enough. Higher incomes do not reliably buy better nutrition (calorie income elasticity of 0 to 0.5), so both must be targeted directly.
  • Market failure. Both have spillovers (a literate neighbour, a non-contagious person), so markets under-provide them and government has a central role.
  • Productivity and poverty. Healthier and better-educated workers earn more (in Brazil a 1% increase in height, a health marker, goes with about 7% higher wages), breaking the vicious circle of poverty, ill health and child labour across generations.
  • Integrated policy. Programmes work best when they link the two: Mexico's Progresa/Oportunidades pays mothers if children attend school and clinics; in Bangladesh the female secondary stipend, immunisation and school feeding work together.

Conclusion: because each multiplies the return on the other, health and education should be planned and financed jointly.
pts: Dual role: ends in themselves (capabilities) and inputs to production (human capital)
Joint investment in the same individual, so each raises the return to the other
Health to education: attendance, learning, longer life raising the return, lower depreciation of education capital
Evidence for the health-education link, for example Kenya deworming (absence down about a quarter, about USD 3.50 per extra school year)
Education to health: literacy for health programmes, hygiene and sanitation, training of health personnel, delayed childbearing
Mothers' education or health knowledge improves child health at any income level
Significance: higher income alone does not deliver health and education (low calorie income elasticity)
Significance: spillovers and market failure justify a strong public role
Significance: integrated programmes, for example Progresa/Oportunidades CCTs or Bangladesh's stipend and immunisation programmes
Significance: higher productivity and wages, and escape from intergenerational poverty
6a.src: Ch 8 Education and health, slides 2-5, 10, 25, 27-28; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 431-437, 470-474
6a.watch:
• "Elaborate their mutual influence" asks for both directions; an answer that covers only health to education earns about half.
  • The 7% wage effect of height is Todaro's figure for Brazil (only about 1% in the United States); it shows the link is strongest among the poor.
  • Bangladesh programmes are illustrations; any correctly described integrated programme earns the credit.

6b.html:
Child labour (ILO) is work by children below the minimum working age (generally 15), or by 15 to 17 year olds in work that threatens their health, safety or morals, or in forced labour.

My opinion: yes, but by stages. The worst forms should be banned and enforced at once; all child labour should be phased out, with support for poor families so that the ban does not push children into worse work.

Arguments for a ban

  1. Harm. Work cuts schooling, stunts growth and exposes children to abuse: the ILO's 2017 report counted 152 million child labourers, 73 million in hazardous work.
  2. Multiple equilibria. Families send children to work only when adult wages are very low, and children substitute (weakly) for adults, so a labour market can have a bad equilibrium (low wage, child labour) and a good one (high wage, none). An effective ban moves it to the good one, where it becomes self-enforcing.
  3. No special skill. Adults are more productive in every task studied; "nimble fingers" is a myth.
  4. Long-run gain. Ending child labour and schooling all children has an estimated return of about 44% (ILO).

Arguments for caution

  1. Poverty. Where the child's wage buys food or school fees, a ban without support leaves the child hungry.
  2. Displacement. Bans and trade sanctions push children into worse informal work, as happened to many dismissed from Bangladesh's garment factories in the 1990s.
  3. Enforcement. Employers resist, and the informal sector is hard to police.

Complementary measures: conditional cash transfers and school stipends (Progresa; Bangladesh's stipends), more and better schools, and poverty reduction, as in the ILO's Worst Forms of Child Labour Convention (1999).

Conclusion: a ban is right, and in a multiple-equilibrium market it makes families better off, but it must be phased and backed by income support and schooling.
pts: Defines child labour (ILO): below the minimum age, or hazardous or forced work for 15 to 17 year olds
States a clear, reasoned opinion (a phased or conditional ban; a reasoned "not immediately" also earns this)
Harm to schooling, health and safety, with ILO evidence (for example 152 million, 73 million in hazardous work)
Multiple-equilibria argument: two equilibria, a ban moves the market to the high-wage one, which is self-enforcing
Children are less productive substitutes for adults (the "nimble fingers" myth)
Counter-argument: poverty, or displacement into worse informal work or the backfiring of trade sanctions, with an example
Complementary policies: CCTs or stipends, school places and quality, poverty reduction, banning the worst forms first
Concludes with a reasoned position consistent with the arguments
6b.src: Ch 8 Education and health, slide 9; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 442-448
6b.watch:
• "Provide your opinion" needs a clear stance; any stance earns the credit if it is argued with evidence and the counter-arguments are answered.
  • The multiple-equilibria case is Todaro's key argument for a ban; without it the answer looks one-sided.
  • The 1990s Bangladesh garment case is widely cited (dismissed children often moved to more dangerous work); give it as an example, not with exact numbers.

7a.html:
The aim of agricultural and rural development is a steady rise in rural living standards, mainly through higher small-farm incomes, output and productivity, together with food security. The slides name three complementary elements: faster farm output growth through technological, institutional and price incentives for small farmers; rising domestic demand for farm output; and labour-intensive non-farm rural activities. The essential components are:

1. Improving small-scale agriculture

  • Technology and innovation. Favour scale-neutral biological and chemical innovations (high-yielding seeds, fertiliser, irrigation), which raise yields on small and large farms alike, over labour-displacing mechanisation where labour is abundant.
  • Research and extension. Public research and extension services reaching small farmers, especially women, who supply 60 to 80% of farm labour in Africa and Asia.
  • Institutional and pricing policies. Fair, market-based farm prices instead of cheap-food policies that favour cities; and access to credit, fertiliser, seed and water for smallholders, not only large landowners, or the Green Revolution widens inequality.
  • Lower risk. Crop insurance, credit and secure tenure (or a larger share for sharecroppers), because risk-averse subsistence farmers rationally reject high-yield but risky techniques.
  • New opportunities and constraints. High-value horticulture, fish and livestock through producer organisations; adaptation to climate change; care with foreign land deals.

2. Conditions for rural development

  • Land reform. Secure tenure and redistribution of land, or tenancy reform (for example West Bengal), so the gains reach those who work the land.
  • Supportive policies. Rural roads, storage, marketing, power and public credit agencies.
  • Integrated objectives. Non-farm jobs and rural industry; education, health, nutrition and housing; less rural inequality and urban-rural imbalance; environmental sustainability (no clearing of forests, careful use of agrochemicals); and a rural sector able to sustain progress.

Bangladesh: high-yielding boro rice with shallow tube-well irrigation, subsidised fertiliser, rural roads and microcredit roughly tripled rice output since independence; now stress-tolerant varieties and crop diversification are needed.

Conclusion: no single measure is enough; technology, incentives, institutions and rural services must come together.
pts: States the objective (small-farm incomes, output, productivity and food security) or the three complementary elements
Technology: scale-neutral biological, chemical and irrigation innovations rather than labour-displacing mechanisation
Research and extension services reaching small farmers, including women
Institutional and pricing policies: fair farm prices (end urban bias) and smallholder access to credit and inputs
Risk reduction for risk-averse farmers (insurance, credit, tenure), or sharecropping reform
New opportunities and constraints: high-value products, producer organisations, climate change
Land reform: secure tenure, redistribution or tenancy reform
Supportive policies: roads, storage, marketing, credit agencies
Integrated rural development: non-farm jobs, social services, less inequality, environmental sustainability
A relevant example, for example Bangladesh's rice Green Revolution or another country
7a.src: Ch 9 Agriculture, slides 2, 8, 19-20, 23, 26; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 524-529
7a.watch:
• "Summarize" asks for the components, not the history of agrarian systems; keep latifundios and minifundios out unless used as a reason for land reform.
  • The Green Revolution technologies are scale-neutral, but the institutions around them often are not; this distinction earns marks.
  • The tripling of rice output is approximate (about 10 to 11 million tonnes in the early 1970s to well over 35 million tonnes now); quote it as "about threefold".

7b.html:
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) is the UN scientific body that assesses climate change. Its reports have three working groups: WG I, the physical science; WG II, impacts, adaptation and vulnerability; WG III, mitigation. The impacts below are mainly WG II findings (the 2007 and 2014 reports).

  1. Water stress. Prolonged droughts, expanding deserts, reduced summer river flow as glaciers retreat (after early floods), and lost or contaminated groundwater; up to a billion people in Asia may face freshwater shortage by the 2050s.
  2. Lower farm output. Grain yields fall in tropical and subtropical areas even with small warming; pests and diseases spread to new ranges; forest and crop fires increase.
  3. Extreme events. More severe storms with heavy rain, flooding and erosion; longer, hotter heat waves; coastal flooding as the sea level rises.
  4. Ecosystems. Damage to freshwater lakes, coastal fisheries, mangroves and coral reefs, and loss of essential species such as pollinators and soil organisms.
  5. Health. Malaria moving to higher altitudes, more diarrhoea and malnutrition, heat deaths; the WHO estimated over 140,000 excess deaths a year by 2004.
  6. Most vulnerable zones. Sub-Saharan Africa (drying), the Asian megadeltas (flooding), small islands, and the Arctic.

Why the poor are hit hardest. They depend on rain-fed farming and natural resources, live in fragile housing on risky land, lack insurance and cannot pay for adaptation. Climate change therefore multiplies poverty and may cause conflict over scarce resources, although rich countries caused most of the emissions.

Bangladesh, an Asian megadelta, faces sea-level rise, salinity in the south-west, stronger cyclones such as Sidr (2007), river floods and climate migration.
pts: Names the IPCC and its working groups (WG I science, WG II impacts and adaptation, WG III mitigation)
Water: droughts, desertification, reduced river flow, groundwater loss or contamination
Agriculture: lower grain yields in the tropics, spreading pests and diseases, fires
Extreme events: severe storms, floods, erosion, heat waves, coastal flooding
Ecosystems: fisheries, mangroves, coral reefs, loss of species
Health: spread of malaria and other diseases, malnutrition, heat deaths
The most vulnerable zones: sub-Saharan Africa, Asian megadeltas, small islands
Why the poor suffer most: rain-fed livelihoods, fragile housing, no insurance, low adaptive capacity; poverty or conflict
Bangladesh or another concrete example
7b.src: Ch 10 Environment, slides 13-15; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 556-559
7b.watch:
• The question asks for impacts, not mitigation policy; carbon taxes and caps belong to WG III and earn nothing here.
  • The slide list (hum-ch10 slide 14) is the core: a student who reproduces it with a short explanation of each impact earns most of the marks.
  • Later IPCC reports (the sixth, 2021-22) confirm and sharpen these findings; any of them is acceptable.

8a.html:
Foreign aid is the transfer of official grants and concessional loans (softer than market terms) to promote development, bilaterally (Japan, China, Russia, India) or through agencies such as the World Bank and ADB.

Role in Bangladesh

  • Two gaps: aid supplemented scarce saving and foreign exchange for reconstruction, food imports and investment.
  • Infrastructure: Jamuna Bridge, power plants, Dhaka Metro Rail (Japan), Rooppur nuclear plant (Russia).
  • Human development: immunisation, family planning (fertility from about 6 to 2.17), school stipends, cyclone shelters, early NGO support (BRAC).
  • Crisis support: budget support, COVID vaccines, the 2023 IMF loan.

Changing pattern: aid fell from roughly 6 to 10% of GNI in the 1970s and 1980s to about 1 to 1.5% now, though disbursement is still large (about USD 10 billion in FY2021-22); loans have replaced grants and food aid.

Problems: tying, conditions, slow disbursement, leakage and rising debt service; the Padma Bridge was self-financed after the World Bank withdrew in 2012.

Conclusion: aid is now a supplement, not the engine of development.
pts: Defines foreign aid: official grants and concessional loans, bilateral or multilateral
Fills the saving and foreign-exchange gaps (reconstruction, food, investment)
Infrastructure role with a named Bangladesh project
Human development role: health, family planning, education, disaster preparedness or NGOs
Changing pattern: falling dependence on aid relative to GNI (no exact figure needed), or the shift from grants to loans
Problems: tying, conditions, slow disbursement, leakage or debt service
Concludes that aid is now a supplement, not the engine of growth
8a.src: Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 806-815; Dimensions of economic development (v3), slides 4, 6; Standard textbook treatment
8a.watch:
• The note's marks are an equal split of the printed 35 for four notes (8.75 each); keep it to about 140 words.
  • The topic has no course slides; the Bangladesh figures (aid share of GNI, FY2021-22 disbursement) are from public World Bank and ERD data, quoted from memory with "about"; any reasonable recent value earns the same credit. The fertility figure 2.17 is hum-dim slide 4 (2023).
  • Do not count private foreign investment or remittances as aid: aid must be non-commercial and concessional.

8b.html:
The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are 17 global goals with 169 targets, adopted by the UN in September 2015 (the 2030 Agenda) for achievement by 2030. They replaced the eight Millennium Development Goals (2000-2015).

New underlying principles

  • Universality: they apply to every nation, rich and poor.
  • Integration: all goals must be achieved together, as they interact.
  • Transformation: structural change, not piecemeal steps.

The goals cover People (1 no poverty, 2 zero hunger, 3 health, 4 education, 5 gender equality), Prosperity (7 energy, 8 decent work, 9 industry, 10 inequality, 11 cities), Planet (6 water, 12 consumption, 13 climate, 14 oceans, 15 land), Peace (16) and Partnership (17). Unlike the MDGs, which aimed to halve poverty, they aim to end it, widen the environmental goals and add inequality and institutions.

Bangladesh: 114th of 167 on the 2025 SDG Index, with only 20.8% of targets on track and a financing gap of about USD 132.6 billion a year.
pts: Defines the SDGs: 17 goals, 169 targets, adopted by the UN in 2015, to be achieved by 2030, successors of the MDGs
States the principles: universality, integration and transformation (or "leave no one behind")
Names the goals, grouped or listed (at least ten goals correctly)
Contrasts with the MDGs: end rather than halve poverty, universal, wider environmental goals, adds inequality and institutions
Gives Bangladesh's status (rank 114, score 63.9, 20.8% of targets on track, or the financing gap)
8b.src: Ch 1 Economic development (Todaro), slides 24-34; Dimensions of economic development (v3), slides 26-28; Bangladesh and the SDGs (2026), slides 3-5, 9, 14
8b.watch:
• The slide gives 26 September 2015; the UN resolution is dated 25 September, during the 25-27 September summit. "September 2015" is safe.
  • Do not confuse goals (17) with targets (169) or indicators (about 230).
  • Marks: Q8 prints 35 for four compulsory short notes, so this note is worth about 8.75.

8c.html:
The Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient measure relative inequality in the size distribution of income.

Lorenz curve. With people ranked from poorest to richest, it plots the cumulative percentage of income against the cumulative percentage of population. The diagonal is the line of perfect equality; the more the curve bows below it, the greater the inequality. In Table 5.1 the bottom 50% gets only 19.8% of income.

Gini coefficient. The area between the diagonal and the curve divided by the whole triangle under the diagonal:

G = \frac{A}{A + B}

It runs from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality); unequal countries lie near 0.50 to 0.70, equal ones near 0.20 to 0.35. Table 5.1 gives 0.44; Bangladesh 0.32 (2010), the United States 0.415 (2016).

Use and limits. A Lorenz curve wholly above another is unambiguously more equal; crossing curves cannot be ranked by this criterion alone. The Gini meets anonymity, scale independence, population independence and the transfer principle.
pts: Lorenz curve: cumulative % of population (poorest first) against cumulative % of income
Diagonal is the line of perfect equality; the further the curve bows below it, the more unequal (an example such as 50% gets 19.8%)
Gini = area between diagonal and curve / total area under the diagonal, A/(A+B)
Range 0 (equality) to 1 (inequality), with typical values or a country example
Lorenz criterion: a higher curve is more equal; crossing curves are ambiguous
Gini meets anonymity, scale independence, population independence and the transfer principle
8c.src: Ch 5 Poverty and inequality, slides 6-15, 34-35, 47; Todaro and Smith, Economic Development, 13th ed., pp 263-269
8c.watch:
• The axes are cumulative; plotting each quintile's own share gives a rising bar chart, not a Lorenz curve.
  • The Gini measures relative inequality only: a poor country and a rich one can have the same value.
  • Two crossing Lorenz curves can even have the same Gini (curves B and C on slide 15).

8d.html:
The Solow growth model (Robert Solow; Mankiw ch 8) explains how saving, population growth and technology determine capital and income per worker in the long run.

Assumptions. Output Y = F(K, L) has constant returns to scale and a diminishing marginal product of capital (MPK). The economy is closed with no government, so Y = C + I. The saving rate s, depreciation rate \delta and labour-force growth rate n are exogenous.

Per worker. With y = Y/L and k = K/L: y = f(k), investment i = s f(k), consumption c = (1-s) f(k).

Equation of motion:

\Delta k = s f(k) - (\delta + n)\,k

Actual investment minus break-even investment (\delta k replaces worn-out capital, nk equips new workers).

Steady state. \Delta k = 0 where s f(k^*) = (\delta + n) k^*; the economy moves to k^* from any starting point.

Results

  • Higher s raises k^* and y^*; growth is faster only during the transition.
  • Higher n lowers k^* and y^*.
  • Golden rule: consumption per worker is highest where \mathrm{MPK} = \delta + n; reaching it requires a policy change in s.

Conclusion. In the steady state y is constant, so lasting growth in living standards must come from technological progress.
pts: Defines the model: long-run growth driven by capital accumulation, saving, population growth and technology
Assumptions: constant returns Y = F(K, L), diminishing MPK, exogenous s, \delta, n
Per-worker form y = f(k) with i = s f(k) and c = (1-s) f(k)
Equation of motion \Delta k = s f(k) - (\delta + n)k, with break-even investment explained
Steady state s f(k^*) = (\delta + n)k^*, stable (in words or on a diagram)
Higher saving raises the level of k^* and y^*, not the steady-state growth rate
Higher population growth lowers k^* and y^*
Golden rule \mathrm{MPK} = \delta + n, or sustained growth needs technological progress
8d.src: Solow model (Mankiw ch 8), slides 5-17, 31-33, 36-46, 50-51; Mankiw, Macroeconomics, ch 8
8d.watch:
• A note without the equation of motion and the steady-state condition misses the core of the model; write both.
  • With technological progress at rate g (Mankiw ch 9), the break-even term becomes (\delta + n + g)k and output per worker grows at g in the steady state; the slides stop at population growth.
  • The slides ask whether the predictions fit the data: across countries, higher investment rates go with higher income per person and faster population growth with lower income.
